header:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Location/Call: Zoom
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Dana Park (Quantified Works - Head of MLOps), Evan Ortiz (Platform Engineer), Priya Menon (CTO)
summary: Intro + qualification on workloads and success metrics. Primary asks: dedicated reserved GPUs with tenant isolation, burst strategy for marketing spikes, private/VPC connectivity questions, and SOC2/KMS compliance. Redwood to send pricing and schedule technical deep dive.
topics: Workload shape and scale; isolation and tenancy model; prewarm and warm pool strategies; burst/fallback policies (hosted fallback); compliance (SOC2, KMS, SSO); cost tradeoffs between dedicated vs hosted and quantization; rollout and canary options.
questions: What level of isolation do we need (full node vs GPU-level)? How do you handle prewarming and cold starts? Can Redwood burst beyond reserved capacity? What's the SLA and pricing structure for Dedicated? How do we route to fallback models when Dedicated saturated?
transcript:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Avery, AE at Redwood, and with me is Marco, our SE. Dana, do you want to kick off with a quick overview of Quantified Works' project and goals?
[00:12] Dana (Quantified Works): Yeah thanks. Uh, hi all. So short version: we run a real-time inference layer for our consumer analytics product. Peak usage is event-driven — marketing campaigns, also end-of-month reporting. We're evaluating Dedicated reserved GPUs because we need predictable latency and some level of tenant isolation for PII-sensitive pipelines.
[00:30] Priya (CTO): And on top of that, we wanna avoid noisy neighbor issues. Right now we have an internal GPU pool but the ops overhead is too high and SRE time is crazy.
[00:40] Marco (Redwood SE): Got it. When you say predictable latency, can you give ballpark QPS and percentiles? That helps us size reserved pools and warm-pool strategy.
[00:48] Evan (Platform Eng): Sure. Baseline is about 25 QPS sustained. Spikes hit 250 QPS for short windows, like 10–30 minutes, maybe twice a week. P95 target is under 120 ms for the main text-gen endpoint, p99 under 350 ms. We also have a batch/async path for heavy jobs.
[01:05] Avery: Important detail — are the spikes synchronous real-time requests or queued jobs? That changes prewarm.
[01:09] Dana: Mostly synchronous, we need responses to feed back to front-end personalization. So we can't fall back to long queues for those spikes.
[01:15] Marco: Ok. So two levers: reserved Dedicated capacity that you own for baseline, plus a burst strategy. Redwood Dedicated can do reserved GPU pools plus burst to hosted or private prewarm pools depending on contract. There are different isolation modes — single-tenant node allocation vs soft tenant fencing. Which do you require?
[01:33] Priya: We prefer node-level isolation for the sensitive pipelines. Some non-PII workloads could be multi-tenant if it keeps costs down.
[01:40] Evan: And we need VPC peering or PrivateLink — no public egress for those flows.
[01:45] Marco: We support VPC peering with private control plane, and for on-prem we can do an air-gapped option. For Dedicated we provide a private network path and you can choose node-level reservation — basically dedicated instances/GPU nodes for your tenancy. There will be a commit for those nodes.
[02:02] Dana: What about burst above the reservation during campaigns? We can't commit to full headroom year-round.
[02:06] Avery: Right, common approach is commit to baseline (say enough GPUs for 25 QPS sustained) and define burst policies for short windows. Two main patterns: 1) Warm pool reserved but pre-warmed with a smaller commit and auto-scaling with prewarmed images, or 2) On-demand burst to hosted capacity with routing and fallbacks. Both have tradeoffs for cost vs latency.
[02:28] Marco: Also quantization — 4-bit or 8-bit quant models — can reduce GPU footprint by 2–3x. That could cut required reserved capacity but might affect P99 latency or quality depending on model.
[02:39] Priya: We need to run a quality gate. If quant causes regressions on our prompt set it's a no-go.
[02:45] Avery: Totally. We usually recommend running an eval harness against your prompt set. Marco can outline perf-vs-quality experiments in the follow-up.
[02:52] Evan: Back to isolation: does node-level reservation guarantee no cross-tenant memory interference and KV cache surprises? We saw KV cache thrash in our K-V cash logs before — sorry, transcription — but memory thrash caused OOMs.
[03:05] Marco: Node-level reservation eliminates noisy neighbor at the GPU/node layer. We also provision separate runtime processes per tenant and can limit KV cache sizes. There are also config knobs for continuous batching thresholds to avoid cross-request contention.
[03:18] Dana: How quickly can prewarm scale? If a campaign triggers a 10x spike, can the warm pool prewarm in under 2 minutes?
[03:26] Marco: Prewarm time depends on model load times and weight residency. For large models ~6–10 minutes for cold starts unless you keep a warm pool always resident. But with warm pools and prefetching KV cache (prefix caching) we can get to steady-state in ~60–90 seconds for many models. For sub-2 minute cold-to-warm you need at least some prewarmed GPUs standing by.
[03:45] Priya: That cost is what worries us — paying for standing warm GPUs. Any hybrid?
[03:49] Avery: You can do a hybrid: reserve minimal warm pool sized for typical spikes, plus enable hosted-burst fallback for extra headroom but route non-sensitive requests there. Sensitive requests always stay on node-isolated capacity.
[04:02] Evan: So routing policy by tag — we can mark routes as sensitive and they won't be routed to hosted. Good.
[04:06] Marco: Exactly. And we can configure automatic fallback routes and priority queuing. In case Dedicated is saturated for non-sensitive traffic, it will overflow to hosted or to a quantized fall-back model variant.
[04:19] Dana: What's the SLA for Dedicated? We need <1% downtime per month and some latency SLOs.
[04:25] Avery: Our Dedicated contracts include an SLA for uptime — enterprise tier, 99.95% typically, and we publish latency baselines based on model family and sequence length. We can include custom SLOs in enterprise terms.
[04:36] Priya: Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS. We need customer-managed keys and audit trails for token access.
[04:44] Marco: We support KMS integrations (customer-managed), HSM in private deployments, and detailed audit logs with token-level tracing in the Redwood Console. SSO and SCIM for RBAC is standard for enterprise accounts.
[04:55] Evan: Also curious about cost modeling. If we reserve N GPUs, do we pay flat monthly regardless of usage? Any burst billing?
[05:02] Avery: Reserved capacity is a commitment — monthly/annual billing for nodes. Burst to hosted is metered; you'd pay additional usage for hosted burst. We can propose mixed pricing: committed discounted rate for reserved pool, and pay-as-you-go rates for burst usage.
[05:17] Dana: For sizing, can we do a short pilot with a small reservation and run traffic, then expand?
[05:22] Marco: Yes, pilot is common. We typically do a 30–60 day pilot on smaller reserved pools to validate latency and cost, then size up. We can also run internal perf benchmarks using your sample payloads.
[05:33] Priya: One more: can Redwood keep model versions pinned per route? We need to control rollouts and do canary tests.
[05:40] Avery: Yes, model pinning, canary rollouts, A/B testing, and automatic fallback policies are supported in the Console. You can pin a major version to Dedicated and route a small percentage to a new variant.
[05:50] Dana: Any examples of customers who do hybrid reserved+hosted and keep sensitive flows private?
[05:55] Avery: We've worked with a couple of fintech and health customers — they reserve node-level pools for sensitive models and have hosted fallback for non-sensitive traffic; we can share anonymized case studies.
[06:04] Evan: About observability — how granular is telemetry? Token-level? Per-route?
[06:09] Marco: Token-level breakdowns, per-route latency histograms, tracing hooks. You can export traces to their APM as well.
[06:16] Priya: Ok, sounds promising. Next steps?
[06:18] Avery: We'll send: 1) Dedicated pricing and commitment tiers; 2) Redwood SOC2 + network diagram and KMS notes; 3) Marco's perf plan and sample payload request; 4) a suggested prewarm/burst playbook that maps your 25->250 QPS shapes to reserved+warm+hosted fallback. We'll also schedule a SE-led perf deep-dive for next week.
[06:36] Dana: Great. Also, can you include rough cost estimates for a hybrid with quantized models vs full precision? That will help our finance team.
[06:43] Marco: Sure — we'll model 8-bit and 4-bit scenarios and show GPU count differences and estimated monthly cost.
[06:49] Priya: Anything else on compliance? We'll share our legal timeline; procurement will probably need a month to review terms.
[06:56] Avery: Noted. We'll also attach a sample SLA and procurement checklist.
[07:00] Dana: Thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[07:03] Avery: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts and set the deep-dive.
[07:07] [Call ends]
notes: Transcript contains minor recognition errors (e.g., K-V cache noted as K V cash). Customer is comfortable with a pilot approach. They emphasized node-level isolation for PII pipelines and hybrid burst strategy. Redwood to deliver pricing, SOC2 and perf plan.
